channel.title: Exoplanet Papers | Daily arXiv Summaries
channel.description: Daily summaries of exoplanet research papers from arXiv astro-ph.EP, written for general audiences.

item.title: The GAPS programme at TNG LXXXII. The first atmospheric investigation of the gas giant WASP-13b at high resolution with GIARPS
item.dc:creator: D. Sicilia et al.
item.description: Why It Matters Some giant planets are astonishingly puffy. WASP-13b is a "hot Jupiter," a gas giant that orbits so close to its star that it reaches about 1500 K (roughly 1200 °C). It is also inflated, about 1.4 times the radius of Jupiter, so it has a very low density, a bit like a cosmic balloon. A puffy atmosphere should be easy to study, because more starlight filters through it when the planet passes in front of its star. Yet many of these planets have barely been examined. Until now, WASP-13b had never been probed with high-resolution spectroscopy, which splits light into fine detail like a prism. What They Did The team used an instrument called GIARPS on the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo (TNG), a telescope in the Canary Islands, to watch four transits, which are the moments the planet crosses in front of its star. They searched the starlight for the fingerprints of helium, hydrogen, sodium, water vapour and carbon monoxide. They also measured how the planet's path sweeps across the spinning star, a technique called the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect. Finally, they planted fake atmospheric signals in the data to test what they would have been able to detect. Key Findings The planet's orbit is well aligned with the star's spin, with a misalignment of just 2.7 ± 1.1 degrees. The star's rotation speed is 4.5 ± 0.1 km per second, more precise than earlier estimates. No clear atmospheric signal showed up. The planted-signal tests rule out an atmosphere that is both rich in heavy elements (about ten times the Sun's level or more) and free of high clouds, meaning clouds sitting above roughly 10 millibar of pressure. The most likely explanation is a layer of high-altitude clouds or haze muting the signals, although a very metal-rich atmosphere cannot be fully excluded. Looking Forward WASP-13b joins a group of puffy hot Jupiters whose spectra look flat and featureless. Seeing through the clouds will take more powerful, next-generation telescopes and instruments.

item.title: Star Cluster Ecology VIII. -- Dynamically Forming S-Type and αCentauri-like Systems
item.dc:creator: Erwan Hochart, Simon Portegies Zwart
item.description: Why It Matters Most stars are born in crowded nurseries, not alone. Picture a busy playground where children bump into each other, pair up and sometimes get pulled apart. Young stars do something similar, and their planets are caught up in the shuffle. Many stars in our galaxy come in pairs, so it is worth asking how planets fare when a partner star appears. The work also asks whether our nearest stellar neighbour, the αCentauri system, could have formed through this kind of cosmic encounter. What They Did The researchers ran computer simulations of a young star cluster modelled on NGC 1333, a real star-forming region. The cluster starts out "sub-virial" (not yet expanding, so stars begin close together and fall toward each other) and "fractal" (clumpy, like clusters within clusters). They tested three setups. In Model A, planetary systems begin in mean motion resonance, meaning the planets' orbits keep a tidy rhythm. In Model B, the same systems are nudged out of that rhythm but stay stable. In Model C, there are no planets at all. Each model was run ten times, following the cluster for 30 million years. Key Findings Pairs of stars formed by chance encounters at similar rates in all three models, so planets barely influence whether such pairs form. The simulations also produced more wide pairs than earlier studies. The authors attribute this to the clumpy, collapsing starting conditions. Planets orbiting just one star of a pair ("S-type") appeared naturally. Planets circling both stars ("P-type") were rare. In Model A, 2% of systems were S-type and 5% were S-type planets in both stars of a binary. Planets thrown out of binary systems left much faster than those thrown out of single-star systems. Collisions between planets and stars, and captures of planets by other stars, happened mostly in binaries. Several αCentauri-like systems appeared, which suggests our nearest neighbour may have formed through such dynamical encounters. Looking Forward The results suggest that binaries and their planets can emerge from the chaos of a star cluster rather than only from the birth of a star. The abstract does not describe specific follow-up plans.

item.title: Assessing PLATO's Discovery Potential across Different Observing Strategies
item.dc:creator: Yoshi Nike Emilia Eschen et al.
item.description: Why It Matters Astronomers have found thousands of planets beyond our solar system, but the ones we know best are large, or they orbit very close to their stars. Planets as small as Earth that take a long time to circle their stars, much like our own world does, are still hard to find. PLATO (PLAnetary Transits and Oscillations of stars), a European space telescope planned to launch in spring 2027, is built to fill this gap. Deciding where it should look, and for how long, will shape what it discovers. What They Did PLATO will first stare at one fixed patch of the Southern sky, called LOPS2, for at least 2 years. After that, it could either keep watching the same patch, for up to 8 years in total, or swing to a Northern patch, LOPN1. LOPN1 overlaps the field watched by the Kepler space telescope. The researchers compared these two plans by estimating how sensitive each would be to small, long-period planets, and how many planets each would likely find. They counted the old Kepler data for the Northern field. They also counted the extra detection power from combining PLATO's observations with those of TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite), which has watched both areas and will keep doing so. Key Findings Watching both fields means looking at more stars, so it gives the largest total number of newly discovered planets. But for small planets and those with long orbits, staying on one field for longer works best. Kepler's old data does sharpen the search in the Northern field. It covers only a fraction of that field and its stars, though, so the improvement for small, long-period planets is only marginal. Looking Forward If the goal is to explore the sparsely charted territory of Earth-sized planets on long orbits, the authors conclude that a longer continuous look at the Southern field, LOPS2, is the best choice. A longer stare is like keeping a camera shutter open longer to catch faint, slow signals. The final decision rests with the mission, but this study gives a clear way to weigh the trade-off.

item.title: "Mega-Earths" are likely an artifact of stellar activity
item.dc:creator: Casey L. Brinkman, Nicolas Cowan
item.description: Why It Matters Astronomers think there is a ceiling on how massive a rocky planet can get. Above about 10 times the mass of Earth, a young planet's core should pull in huge amounts of gas and snowball into a gas giant, rather than staying rocky. Yet a handful of planets seem to be both extremely heavy and dense enough to be made of rock, like Earth. If real, these "Mega-Earths" would force scientists to rethink how planets form. What They Did The researchers looked at the ultra-massive rocky planets reported in the scientific literature and asked what they have in common. Every one of them orbits a magnetically active star, meaning one with a restless surface. Activity is measured by a number called logR'HK (a gauge of a star's glow from magnetic activity), and for these stars it is above -4.75. The team calculated how likely it would be for all of these planets to end up around such stars purely by chance. They also searched for any physical reason why giant rocky planets would prefer active stars. Key Findings They found less than a 1% probability that the pattern is a coincidence. They also found no astrophysical reason to expect Mega-Earths to form preferentially around active stars. They conclude that Mega-Earths are most likely artifacts of stellar activity. In other words, the star's own behavior may be fooling the measurements, much like trying to hear a faint whisper next to a loud, unpredictable radio. The authors also question how reliable Gaussian Processes are for measuring the masses of rocky planets around active stars. This statistical technique is used to separate a star's activity "noise" from the tiny signal a planet leaves behind. Looking Forward If this conclusion holds, the apparent exceptions to the 10-Earth-mass limit may disappear, and the standard picture of planet formation would stay intact. It also suggests that mass measurements of rocky planets around active stars deserve extra caution and a closer look at the methods used to obtain them.

item.title: The Hydrological Cycle and Circulation of Tidally-Locked Planets with a Finite Moisture Inventory
item.dc:creator: Daniel A. Williams et al.
item.description: Why It Matters Many planets orbiting small, dim stars are "tidally locked." Like the Moon facing Earth, they keep one side in permanent daylight and the other in permanent night. Their weather looks nothing like ours, with planet-wide air flows and fast jet streams. Whether such a world can hold liquid water matters a great deal for judging whether it could support life. The risk is that water evaporates on the hot day side, travels to the night side, and freezes there for good, leaving the sunny side a desert. What They Did The researchers ran idealised computer simulations of a planet's atmosphere, known as general circulation models (GCMs). These are simplified versions of the software used for weather and climate forecasts. They varied the total amount of water available at the surface, from small to large, and watched how the water cycle of evaporation, clouds, rain and runoff evolved. They also changed the threshold at which evaporation starts to slow because the surface liquid is running low. Key Findings With little water, the planet quickly develops a barren day side and a wet night side where the moisture gets trapped. With more water, the drying of the day side is significantly delayed. A lake forms just east of the point directly beneath the star. A permanent thunderstorm-like system keeps it supplied, and the storm persists even after the lake itself has vanished. The lake takes thousands of years to disappear. Even a weak process returning moisture from the night side to the day side could therefore keep the day side moist. The evaporation threshold also changes how long the lake and the surrounding conditions last. Looking Forward These results suggest that the distribution of water, and the presence of a lake under the star, may shape the climate and habitability of tidally locked worlds. The study uses idealised simulations, so real planets may differ. Even so, it points to where astronomers might look for signs of moisture on these planets.

item.title: The origin of the large heavy element contents of warm Jupiters
item.dc:creator: Bertram Bitsch
item.description: Why It Matters Warm Jupiters are giant planets that orbit their stars fairly closely, but not as scorchingly close as "hot" Jupiters. Models of their interiors show that many are packed with "heavy elements," meaning everything heavier than hydrogen and helium, such as rock, metal, and ices. In some cases these elements make up as much as 30-40% of the planet's mass. That is surprising, because giant planets are mostly made of hydrogen and helium gas. Working out how these planets collected so much heavy material helps us understand how planetary systems, possibly including our own, are built. What They Did The researchers used a computer code called chemcomp. It simulates how planets grow and move inside the disc of gas and dust around a young star. The key idea is "pebble drift and evaporation." Small pebbles of ice and rock drift inward toward the star. When they get warm enough, the ices turn to vapor and enrich the inner disc's gas with heavy elements. Water ice evaporates fairly close to the star, while carbon dioxide, methane, and carbon monoxide evaporate farther out. A planet that grows from or swallows this enriched gas can take in a lot of heavy material. The team simulated planets that form and migrate through discs of different sizes, around stars of different masses and metal content. Key Findings Pebble drift and evaporation can explain the wide range of heavy element contents found in giant planets. Larger discs keep up a strong flow of pebbles for longer, so planets there collect more heavy elements. Planets that form or move inside the water ice line gain more heavy elements from the vapor-enriched gas than planets formed farther out. Stars rich in metals help inner-disc planets become more enriched, but planets forming in the outer disc stay much less enriched whatever the metal content. Stellar mass matters only slightly when disc size and mass are the same. Looking Forward The authors suggest that the observed trend of heavier planets holding more heavy elements comes from two things combined: discs of different sizes, and warm giants that originate in either the inner or outer disc. Future observations of planet interiors and compositions can test this picture.

item.title: Detailed study of HD 219134: a benchmark K-dwarf with a compact planetary system
item.dc:creator: Jérôme Bétrisey et al.
item.description: Why It Matters To understand a planet, you first have to understand its star. If we misjudge the star's size, we misjudge the planets circling it. HD 219134 is a nearby orange dwarf star, cooler and smaller than our Sun, with a tightly packed family of planets. That makes it a "benchmark," a reference object that scientists use to test their methods. But two different ways of measuring its size disagreed. Interferometry combines light from several telescopes to directly measure the star's width. Asteroseismology reads the star's natural vibrations, a bit like judging a bell's size from its ring. The mismatch needed to be settled. What They Did The team built computer models of the star and fitted them to its vibration patterns. They also used "seismic inversions," a technique that works backward from the vibrations to the star's interior. They tested how different assumptions changed the answers. They then used the updated star properties to reconstruct how its spin, magnetic activity, stellar wind, and high-energy X-ray output changed over billions of years, and what that meant for its planets. Key Findings The inversions rule out the most recent interferometric radius, while the 2019 interferometric measurement agrees with the vibration results. The star has a mass of 0.779 ± 0.015 times the Sun's, a radius of 0.753 ± 0.005 solar radii, and an age of about 8.92 ± 0.89 billion years. Standard models of magnetic braking, the gradual slowing of a star's spin, broadly match its present rotation, though weaker braking fits slightly better. The X-ray history suggests the innermost planets lost their atmospheres early, while the outer planets probably kept part of their original gas envelopes. HD 219134d lost only a moderate amount. The authors think the earlier interferometric uncertainties were underestimated. Looking Forward The authors recommend adopting the asteroseismic radius, which held up under different modeling choices. A trustworthy size for this star gives a firmer base for studying its planets' composition and history, and for calibrating similar stars.
